extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers writing mathematics and technical papers (graduate students, academic authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and presenting mathematical writing: notation and proofs, use of illustrations/tables/quotes, preparing manuscripts for publication, and interacting with editors. Emphasis on clarity, appropriate examples, and good exposition practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams should be kept small
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrams are good if they are kept small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small diagrams are preferable; fold-out or very large diagrams can be useful (examples: fold-out syntax chart, fold-out comparison of sort-on-tapes performances) but are exceptional. Detailed figures are acceptable if the detail is there for readers who want it but can be ignored by others; be aware referees may complain that a figure is 'too detailed'. Use diagrams to make opaque prose clear — if an account is hard to follow, a diagram often helps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use real data rather than contrived sample data
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to use 'real' data than 'sample data' that have in fact been cooked up solely to use as an example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose authentic, representative examples to illustrate algorithms or behavior (Knuth used a paragraph from Grimms' Fairy Tales as test data). Real data demonstrate typical behavior and avoid misleading artifacts that arise from contrived examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include quantitative illustrative measures where helpful
rubrics_metrics.description: When describing processes (e.g., line-breaking), print the numerical measures illustrating the effect alongside the typeset example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show real numbers (e.g., amounts of stretch/compression for each line) beside the rendered example; deliberately include extreme/bad examples to show what goes wrong (and inform printers when an example's appearance is intentionally 'wrong'). These artifacts make the exposition concrete and informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose representation appropriate to the phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the form of illustration that best conveys the essential features (sometimes a listing of events is best; sometimes a diagram; sometimes a table).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: asynchronous processes may be best conveyed by a listing of events rather than a diagram (Caltech elevator states). For complex algorithmic interactions (overlaps, rewinds, buffering) a well-designed diagram can capture subtleties that textual analysis misses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use running examples to compare methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the same running example across many presentations/algorithms to show contrasts (e.g., 16 numbers sorted by dozens of algorithms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single, consistent example lets readers directly compare outputs or behaviors of different algorithms/techniques and makes graphical comparisons more meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use histograms/scattergrams and disclose biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Use histograms and scattergrams to illustrate distributions and multi-dimensional data, but acknowledge biases introduced by data selection or re-writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knuth printed histograms showing how often T E X generated more-or-less distorted lines and explained that his rewriting of particularly ugly paragraphs biased the results. State any known bias or selection process so readers can interpret the visualizations properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with visual scaling and deceptive graphics
rubrics_metrics.description: Visuals can mislead (How to Lie with Statistics); perceived magnitudes depend on visual encoding (e.g., area vs. height).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose scales and encodings that honestly represent quantities. The example: representing a 17% height increase by showing volumes (sacks) exaggerates perceived change—be aware of such perceptual pitfalls (Tufte, Huff).

rubrics_metrics.name: Color: effective in talks, usually not in papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Color can be used effectively in talks, but usually not in papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve color for live presentations where it enhances comprehension; avoid relying on color in printed papers (printing costs, legibility, reproduction issues). If color is essential, consider how it will reproduce in the publication medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrations increase production effort drastically
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of work involved in preparing a paper for publication is proportional to the cube of the number of illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect significantly more preparation and production time as illustrations increase. Plan accordingly and justify each figure; complex multi-color or numerous figures multiply effort for both author and publisher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical tables have unique value
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerical tables can sometimes present ideas that can't be demonstrated graphically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tables when they convey patterns or precise numeric behavior (e.g., oscillations) that visuals cannot easily show. Place explanatory text opposite the diagrams to which it refers to guide readers efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange text opposite referenced diagrams
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure the final text is arranged opposite the diagrams to which it refers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place explanatory text near its figure to reduce reader effort and confusion. During layout, ensure captions and references align with the associated illustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give proper credit and acknowledgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge contributors properly; young authors frequently overlook proper acknowledgments in their haste to publish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List coauthors, illustrators, and contributors appropriately. Omitting credits harms colleagues and can be seen as a serious oversight; conversely, well-known examples (Erdős naming a porter) illustrate generous crediting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize complicated notation (avoid nested subscripts/superscripts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for notation that needs no double subscripts or subscripted superscripts; simplify notation where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recast proofs to reduce heavy indexing; prefer readable notation or plain English when it improves clarity. The assignment explicitly asked for notation with no subscripted subscripts or subscripted superscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay explicit enumeration when possible ('hold back')
rubrics_metrics.description: Hold back before enumerating the elements of a set; you can say that S is countable without writing S = {s1, s2, ...}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using words instead of early formal notation can make exposition clearer. Introduce specific notation only when it helps; this reduces cognitive load for the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor proofs into subgoals and give orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor proofs into parts: describe a subgoal that captures the crucial property, then present the final step (coup de grâce). Give an orientation like 'this is essentially a diagonalization technique'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factored proofs are easier to follow because each piece has a simple interface. Explicitly naming the technique or structure used helps reader comprehension (e.g., state that a proof is diagonalization-based). Also consider addressing initialization or special base cases to avoid grader/readability objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer words over heavy notation when clearer
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes words are superior to notation; avoid unnecessary notational correspondences when plain English suffices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solution B (and C) showed that describing counterparts in words or using sequences of ordered pairs can avoid cumbersome formal correspondences and improve readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples and diagrams to reveal algorithmic trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: When describing algorithmic choices, illustrate trade-offs (e.g., demerit cutoffs speed algorithms but can miss solutions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how practical heuristics (like demerit cutoffs limiting nodes per level) affect completeness/performance and show with diagrams/analysis when such shortcuts might exclude desirable solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for editorial changes and check proofs carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors may rewrite style and introduce errors; authors should check proofs, especially for technical/typographical math.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect editorial changes and be prepared to re-edit. Insist on seeing galley proofs for math-heavy manuscripts, correct introduced errors, and negotiate on style/content decisions. Use proof stage to catch printer-induced or copy-editor alterations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be meticulous about captions and fit in publication layouts
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions and figure text may be adjusted by editors to fit layout; these edits can change meaning or remove words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review caption edits carefully; minor deletions (e.g., removing 'the's to make lines fit) can alter clarity. Where layout constraints are tight, work with editors to preserve intended meaning while achieving fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quotation judiciously — don't quote to show off
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation due to the motive 'to show that he is learned and well-read' is invariably ill-advised; use quotations because they convey meaning better or are apt/beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search systematically (Bartlett, OED, concordances) for apt quotations; quote yourself if necessary. Prefer quotations that genuinely illuminate or frame the discussion rather than impress readers. Keep quotations relevant and appropriately sourced.
